title: Build Your First Nodics Capability
readerIntent: Understand the safe end-to-end path for adding one project-owned business capability.
priorKnowledge: Complete the local setup and understand basic APIs and data models.
summary: Start with ownership and contracts, reuse existing capabilities, add only necessary layers, and prove positive and rejected behavior.

sections.heading: What this tutorial teaches
paragraphs: This tutorial teaches the decision sequence for adding business behavior safely. It does not encourage creating every possible layer. A small capability may need only configuration, a schema, and an existing CRUD contract; a complex capability may also need services, facades, APIs, events, jobs, workflows, search, and import/export.
The example is a tenant-owned service request managed by authorized employees. Replace its business fields with your project requirement while preserving the ownership and verification process.

sections.heading: Prerequisites and starting state
items: A verified local Nodics runtime and clean baseline tests.
A customer or application project layer separate from reusable Nodics framework source.
A tenant and authorized employee test identity.
A clear statement of the user outcome, data sensitivity, lifecycle, integrations, and expected scale.
Agreement about which existing capability owns related identity, tenant, workflow, search, or notification behavior.

sections.heading: Example outcome
paragraphs: Imagine a project needs tenant-owned service requests that authorized employees can create, view, update, and close. Treat that outcome as one project capability rather than scattering it across framework modules.

sections.heading: Describe the contract before files
items: Business identity: a stable request code and a human-readable description.
Scope: tenant ownership, optional enterprise relationship, and employee permissions.
Lifecycle: open, assigned, resolved, and closed states with allowed transitions.
Relationships: requester, assignee, contacts, attachments, or other owned models.
Operations: create, search, view, update, assign, resolve, close, and audit.
Failures: invalid fields, duplicate identity, missing relation, forbidden tenant, forbidden transition, unavailable dependency, and concurrency conflict.
Non-functional behavior: observability, performance, retention, privacy, import/export, and customization.

sections.heading: Implementation sequence
items: Search for an existing authority and extension point.
Choose the project module that owns the capability.
Describe data, permissions, tenant ownership, states, integrations, failures, and customization.
Add schema, service, API, configuration, event, or pipeline layers only when each has a responsibility.
Regenerate derived artifacts from source definitions.
Update canonical documentation and the concise module README.

sections.heading: Choose the owning project module
paragraphs: The owning module must be loader-visible in the customer project and active in the intended runtime. It owns the service-request schema, business service, API contract, configuration namespace, tests, and implemented documentation.

Profile continues to own employees and tenants. Workflow continues to own workflow execution. Search providers continue to own search-engine integration. The new capability refers to those contracts instead of copying their schemas or connecting directly to their storage.

sections.heading: Model data and relationships
items: Reuse the framework base behavior that is merged at runtime rather than repeating inherited metadata without need.
Define fields, types, required behavior, indexes, uniqueness, defaults, validation, permissions, and ownership in the owning schema contract.
Represent relationships through supported model references and decide whether related records may be selected, created, or only viewed.
Keep configurable permissions and ownership policy in the owning properties namespace when later project layers must customize them.
Allow database modules to generate and operate persistence models; do not add direct database-driver access to the business capability.

sections.heading: Add business behavior and API exposure
paragraphs: Place reusable business rules in the service layer. Use a facade when an operation coordinates several services or capabilities. Controllers translate transport input and output; routers define versioned exposure and security metadata. Pipelines and interceptors handle reusable cross-cutting lifecycle behavior.
Do not place business rules in Axis, another frontend, package metadata, generated files, or a convenience utility that has no ownership.

sections.heading: Configuration and customization
items: Put application behavior in properties.js under a capability-owned namespace, not in package.json.
Provide safe defaults and document which project, environment, server, node, tenant, or runtime layers may override them.
Validate configuration at startup or activation and fail with actionable status information.
Keep credentials external to committed properties.
Prove a later project layer can customize an intended rule without editing the original implementation.

sections.heading: Generated artifacts
paragraphs: Schemas and route definitions may produce models, services, API descriptions, tests, reports, and AI context. The source definition remains authoritative. Regenerate after a contract change and inspect the result; do not fix generated output by hand.
A default sample file created by module scaffolding is not a required business-service name and must not be filled merely to satisfy a structural assumption.

sections.heading: Verification
items: Successful create, read, update, and close behavior.
Missing and invalid information.
Unauthorized and wrong-tenant access.
State boundaries such as closing an already closed request.
Later project-layer customization.
Contract, integration, generated-artifact, and regression behavior.

sections.heading: Run an end-to-end example
items: Authenticate an authorized employee in the default test tenant.
Create a request with a stable code, description, and valid requester relation.
Search for the request and verify its friendly display fields.
Assign and resolve it through allowed transitions.
Attempt the same operations as an unauthorized employee and with a wrong-tenant context.
Close the request and confirm repeated close is rejected or handled idempotently according to the contract.
Review logs, status codes, audit context, generated contracts, and database state.

sections.heading: Documentation required for completion
items: A beginner overview explaining the capability and business outcome.
Business value, personas, concepts, lifecycle, and a recognizable example.
Developer configuration, schema, service, API, relationship, extension, and test guidance.
Operator health, diagnostics, failure, performance, backup, and recovery guidance.
Technical reference linked to current source evidence.
A concise module README that identifies ownership and points to canonical documentation instead of duplicating it.

sections.heading: What not to do
items: Do not modify reusable framework code for a customer-only rule.
Do not create a second loader, registry, workflow, or persistence authority.
Do not edit generated artifacts as the long-term source.
Do not declare completion while tests or documentation are stale.

sections.heading: Expected result
paragraphs: The project now owns one understandable capability that runs through normal Nodics loading, configuration, persistence, security, API, testing, and documentation contracts. It can be used by a separate frontend and customized through an approved later layer.

If achieving the result required a second loader, direct database connection, copied identity model, frontend business rule, or manual generated-file edit, revisit the ownership decision before building further.

sections.heading: Complete guide: Build Your First Nodics Capability
paragraphs: This journey is for someone who understands basic programming but is new to Nodics. It explains the whole path before asking you to learn each internal detail.

sections.heading: What You Will Build
paragraphs: Imagine that a business needs to keep a list of service requests. A user should be able to create a request, view it, update it, and close it. Different customers must not accidentally access each other's information.
In Nodics, this business idea becomes one owned **capability**. A capability is a coherent piece of business behavior with one clear home.

sections.heading: The Five Pieces In Plain Language
paragraphs:
| Nodics term | Plain-language meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Module | The home that owns the capability. |
| Schema | The agreed shape and rules for the information. |
| Service | The business behavior performed on that information. |
| Route/API | The controlled doorway used by another application. |
| Test | Executable evidence that the behavior and its boundaries work. |
You may later use controllers, facades, pipelines, events, or providers. Do not add them merely because they exist. Add a layer when it owns a clear responsibility.

sections.heading: Step 1: Confirm The Capability Owner
paragraphs: Search the [Module Documentation Index](/docs/reference/modules) and [Complete Module Catalog](/docs/reference/modules). Extend an existing capability when it already owns the behavior. Create a new project module only when the business capability is genuinely new.
Do not place customer behavior in a reusable framework module. Nodics framework modules supply defaults; project modules own project behavior and overrides.

sections.heading: Step 2: Describe The Contract Before Coding
paragraphs: Write down:
This short description prevents the API, data model, and permissions from becoming separate guesses.
items: the information the service request contains;
who may create, read, update, or close it;
which tenant owns it;
valid and invalid states;
whether another module or external system is involved;
how success and failure will be observed;
which behavior a customer may customize.

sections.heading: Step 3: Put Each Concern In Its Owned Layer
paragraphs: Use [How To Create Application Functionality](/docs/build/application-capability) for the detailed workflow. In summary:
environments may change.
items: Define data rules in the owning module's schema definitions.
Define business behavior in its service layer.
Expose only the required API operations through route definitions.
Configure permissions and tenant behavior explicitly.
Use layered `properties.js` configuration for policy that projects or
Keep generated files generated from their source definitions.

sections.heading: Step 4: Verify More Than The Happy Path
paragraphs: Test:
Follow [How To Test Nodics Changes](/docs/build/testing) for the available test and generation commands.
items: a valid service request;
missing or invalid information;
a user without permission;
access from the wrong tenant;
state boundaries, such as closing an already closed request;
project-level customization;
the API and generated contract;
integration with any module or provider involved.

sections.heading: Step 5: Make The Capability Discoverable
paragraphs: Update the owning module README with purpose, ownership, configuration, extension points, security, and verification. Update `gDocs` when users need a new task guide. Update AI/developer contracts when the implementation rule or extension boundary changes.

sections.heading: What Success Looks Like
paragraphs: A new developer should be able to answer all of these without reading every source file:
items: What business problem does the capability solve?
Which module owns it?
Which API and data contract does it expose?
Who may use it?
How is tenant separation preserved?
How may a project customize it?
Which tests prove it?
What must be regenerated after a change?
